analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour over four years, then indexes it to median wages.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill gathered 57 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats, but was never given a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps — from $9 an hour to $10.50, $12, $13.50, and finally $15 over four years — and then adjusted it each year with the growth in the median hourly wage so it would not erode. It would also have gradually closed the lower 'tip credit' wage for tipped workers until they earned the same minimum as everyone else, guaranteed that workers keep their tips, and raised the separate lower wage allowed for teenage new hires. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 15-plus million workers projected by advocates to be affected, chiefly adults in retail, food service, and care work earning between the current $7.25 minimum and $15 an hour, including tipped workers who would eventually get the full minimum in cash wages.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in five steps to $15 an hour, beginning at $9.00, then $10.50, $12.00, $13.50, and $15.00 over four years.

After reaching $15, the minimum would rise each year by the percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all employees, so it keeps pace with typical pay rather than eroding until Congress acts again.

Phases out the lower cash wage for tipped employees, raising it by up to $1.50 a year until it equals the standard minimum, so tipped workers' base pay would no longer depend on tips to reach minimum wage.
Gives employees an explicit legal right to retain their tips and requires employers to inform them of that right.
Requires the Labor Department to publish each scheduled wage increase 60 days before it takes effect, so employers and workers have advance notice.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage — especially restaurants, retail, and other labor-intensive businesses — through higher payroll costs, and indirectly some consumers through higher prices; some low-wage workers could also face reduced hours or slower hiring under employers' objections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Minimum-wage employers, especially restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps a subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, allowing employers to pay the standard minimum minus $3.00 an hour for their first 90 days — less than the adult minimum throughout the phase-in.

Raising the wage floor to $15 nationwide is a steep, fast increase for some low-wage regions and industries; employer groups argued it would cost jobs, cut hours, or push some businesses to automate, and the bill included no small-business tax offsets to soften the transition.
Eliminating the tip credit changes a compensation structure many restaurants and some tipped workers defended, forcing employers to pay the full minimum in cash wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: a large, reliable raise for the lowest-paid workers, paid for mostly by their employers and their customers. The step-by-step schedule and advance-notice rules give businesses time to adjust, but a national $15 floor is a bigger jump for low-cost rural areas than for cities, and the bill offers no offsetting relief for small employers. On balance, the direct benefits to low-wage workers — including the phase-out of the tipped subminimum — outweigh the acknowledged adjustment costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Ellison introduced the bill on July 22, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On November 16, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 114th Congress.
Fifty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill in addition to its sponsor; no Republican signed on.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage, particularly restaurant and retail chains, were better off because the wage increase never advanced; the congressional majority that controlled the committee schedule avoided a vote it could have lost politically.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers and the majority that buried it

sides.party_line_note: All 57 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican majority that controlled the committee never allowed it a vote.

industries.note: Restaurants would pay the full minimum in cash wages to tipped workers as the tip credit phased out, plus much higher wages for their lowest-paid staff. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the raise their workers would have gained.
Businesses with large minimum-wage workforces would bear the payroll increases. The industry's interest in stopping the bill was the mirror image of its workers' interest in passing it.

The bill raises the youth subminimum over time (the minimum minus $3.00 eventually reaches $12), but preserves a lower wage for under-20 workers during their first 90 days, so young new hires gain less than adult minimum-wage workers.
